newsitem.title: USA: Miami witness cites cartel ties to Colombia's Samper.
newsitem.headline: Miami witness cites cartel ties to Colombia's Samper.

text.p: Before Ernesto Samper was elected president of Colombia in 1994, he and his running mate Humberto de la Calle had dinner with leaders of the Cali cocaine cartel, a former accountant for the gang testified at a drugs trial in Miami on Wednesday.

Guillermo Pallomari testified that Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, who headed the infamous Colombian drug gang with his brother Gilberto, told him he was holding the dinner meeting with the politicians to discuss the terms under which he might surrender to government authorities.
"It (the dinner) was discussed afterward at a meeting where I heard Mr. Miguel Rodriguez say that the situation regarding their surrender was going well with Mr. Samper," Pallomari said.

Pallomari, who served as the cartel's accountant and said he also was Miguel Rodriguez's personal assistant, is the star witness in the U.S. case against two American lawyers, one of them a former Justice Department official, and four accused South Florida smugglers on charges of obstructing justice and drug trafficking.

During his five days of testimony, Pallomari has said the cartel had agents infiltrated throughout the Colombian government. On Tuesday, he testified that the cartel had funnelled at least $5 million into Samper's presidential campaign, with Rodriguez boasting to subordinates after Samper's victory: "We have a president!"
On Wednesday, he described how cartel agents sent Rodriguez copies of confidential documents from the attorney general's and chief prosecutor's offices, Colombia's congress and other agencies.

Pallomari's testimony marks the first time a witness for the U.S. government has alleged that the Samper campaign and other Colombian politicians took bribes to pass laws that favoured drug traffickers, although corruption has been alleged by Colombian officials.

"The Cali cartel had infiltrated people into all individual government agencies, people who worked for the Cali cartel," Pallomari said. "They would turn over documents of interest to them (cartel leaders)."

Samper has responded to Pallomari's allegations by saying the Miami trial is merely repeating charges the Colombian congress reviewed last year when it cleared him of using drug money to finance his election campaign.
"It's the same movie -- but in English," he told reporters in Colombia.

The trial in Miami came after a four-year U.S. probe of the Cali cocaine cartel that investigators said uncovered shipments of hundreds of thousands of tons of cocaine into the United States. The original indictment charged 59 people, including six lawyers, with involvement in the drug trade.

On trial are Michael Abbell, who was chief of the U.S. Justice Department's Office of International Affairs during the Reagan administration; William Moran, a criminal defence attorney and former prosecutor; and four men U.S. officials charge helped warehouse and ship drugs -- Luis Grajales, Eddie Martinez, Ramon Martinez and Jose Herrera Solas.
